decision: Bounded deterministic and partial-rejection qualification passed for tested fixtures; retain current production profile pending isolation and representative stress gates.
measured_scope: Same frozen PTQ1 runtime/model, c32768, slot1, FAon, t8, no CPU binding, same seed42/temp0. Three matched OpenAI buffered requests for each of count/tool/ordinal per profile, preceded by one warmup per case. Corpus streaming disabled and stream_options removed for complete native timing objects. Count/ordinal max256, tool max128; actual completions183/256/39.
partial_rejection_evidence: Ordinal fixed8:255 proposed/214 accepted in each formal repeat; adaptive237/213 then239/215 twice. Exact payload digests match none for all repeats. This exercises a partial-reject path on qwen35 for this 256-token fixture; it is not a proof for all recurrent states or context lengths.
digest_caveat: Canonical JSON of exact content plus tool type and full function object; only engine-generated random tool-call id omitted. Original full message digest is also recorded; no text/arguments normalization is applied to digest.
limits: Repeated warmups and identical requests may train/preserve ngram history. cache_prompt=false and cache_n0 do not prove ngram dictionary isolation or cold-history gains.
Corpus count/tool and ordinal are a bounded small fixture set. Do not advertise synthetic2.2x as general workload speedup.
Per-tenant cache isolation, cancellation cleanup, long-context rollback and concurrent slot/profile compatibility remain production gates.
Adaptive improved the ordinal median relative to fixed8 while fixed8 was faster on count/tool and pure repetition. No universal winner is established.
Tool semantics passed bench_sum name and a19/b23 arguments; original random-id-sensitive full message digests remain in raw evidence.
No CUDA graph or kernel trace was collected. This is direct engine evidence, not Power/Gateway E2E performance.
supersedes: p4-statement.json remains accurate for its initial repetitive fixture only; its partial-reject limitation is addressed narrowly by this follow-up, not globally.
